amendments.rule: Where **one Greek noun** is rendered by an English adjective-plus-noun phrase, rule 17's head turns on whether the English **noun** is itself a gloss of the lexeme or a supplied generic completion. Where the noun glosses it, the noun is the head: `εὐδοκία` → *good pleasure*, `εὐνοία` → *good will*, `εὐαγγέλιον` → *good tidings*, `ζῷον` → *living creature*, `ἀρχιερεύς` → *chief priest* and *high priest*, `κτίσμα` → *created thing*, `ἀποκαραδοκία` → *earnest expectation*. Where it is a generic completion and another word carries the sense, that word is the head: `πλεονέκτης` → *covetous man* heads on *covetous*, as `ἀγάπαις` → *love feasts* heads on *love*, `πραιτώριον` → *praetorian guard* on *praetorian*, and `σπουδή` → *earnest care* on *earnest*, the corpus glossing that lexeme *diligence* and never *care*. This is rule 17's generic-noun clause holding for a noun rather than a substantival adjective or demonstrative, and the same test it already applies to `all things` and `good thing`. Do not decide it from English syntax: rule 17 forbids choosing a word merely because it is the phrase's formal head, which is the only thing *care* or *man* could rely on. The phrase need not be adjective-plus-noun for this test, and the ASV's word order does not change it. Where the ASV renders one Greek **compound** noun by two English words **each of which glosses one of its elements**, the head is the word answering to the compound's **nominal core** and not the one answering to its modifying or prefixed element, even where English syntax makes that modifier the phrase's formal head and puts the core in a complement: `πιθανολογίᾳ` → *persuasiveness of speech* heads on *speech* and `ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ` → *will worship* on *worship*, as rule 91's `καταλαλιάς` → *evil speakings* heads on *speakings* and `δυσφημίας` → *evil report* on *report*, and as rule 104's `εὐπειθής` → *easy to be entreated* and `εὐάρεστος` → *well pleasing* head their stem words. That is this rule's own line held to and not an exception to it: `εὐδοκία`, `εὐνοία` and `εὐαγγέλιον` all head the core and never the `εὐ-`. So ask first whether **both** English words gloss something, and only then which of them is the core; where one of them glosses no element at all the generic-completion arm decides it instead, which is why *man* and *feasts* lose to *covetous* and *love*. Rule 46 is untouched, because `χάριν` is a postposition rather than a noun and the supplied *cause* or *sake* is what carries its sense, and rules 22, 49 and 58 are untouched, because there the supplied word answers to an article or determines a phrase rather than completing a noun's own English expression.
amendments.why: Rule 66 as it stood decided the head by asking whether the English noun glosses the lexeme, and its examples all had the glossing word standing as the English phrase's formal head, so it never faced a rendering where the two come apart. COL.2 met that case twice and analysed it two ways — ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ → will worship on worship at 2.23, πιθανολογίᾳ → persuasiveness of speech on persuasiveness at 2.4 — which is the split this pass patched. The added clause states the test the patch rests on and closes the gap in the rule's own voice rather than leaving the unqualified sentence for the next reader. The corpus is uniform behind it: rule 91's καταλαλιάς and δυσφημίας rows, rule 104's εὐ- compounds, and rule 66's own εὐδοκία, εὐνοία, εὐαγγέλιον and ἀρχιερεύς all head the core element, and the four rows that head a modifier (πλεονέκτης, ἀγάπαις, πραιτώριον, σπουδή) are every one of them a case where the English noun glosses no element, which the amendment says in terms.

amendments.rule: The ASV's supplied appositional ***even*** — the italicized word that introduces an appositive English marks by apposition rather than by a conjunction — is decided by the **class of the Greek token that carries the appositive it introduces**, and not by the ASV's italics, which rule 11 makes evidence rather than a verdict. Where an **expressed preposition** carries it, *even* folds onto that preposition as a rule 7 helper headed on the prepositional word: `ἐκ` → *even from* at GAL.1.15 and *even of* at JAS.4.1, `εἰς` → *even unto* at 2CO.10.16, `διά` → *even by* at 2CO.1.19, and `ἐν` → *even in* at GAL.5.14 and 1JN.5.20, as the improper prepositions do at PHP.2.8, REV.12.11, REV.14.20, REV.18.5 and 2CO.12.2 — ten units, none `added`, and no `added` bare *even* anywhere in the corpus stands where a preposition introduces the appositive. Where a **substantival article** carries it, *even* is its own `added` unit under rule 5 headed on itself, and the article keeps only its bare pronoun: `ὁ` → *he* at 1JN.2.22, JHN.1.27 and JAS.4.12, as `τοῖς` → *to them* at JHN.1.12, `τοὺς` → *them that* at REV.13.6 and `τὰ` → *the things that were* at REV.16.3 do, and as an articular appositive does at 1JN.2.25, JHN.3.13, REV.20.14, EPH.2.15 and JHN.15.26. Rule 32's *and nothing else* is what decides that side, rule 90 relaxing the phrase only for a **relativizer**, which is pronoun and relativizer at once, where *even* is neither; 1JN.2.25 states the positive reason and it is the whole distinction between the two carriers — a case preposition rides with an article because it realizes the article's **own case**, and *even* realizes nothing. So the article carrier is settled in rule 71's shape rather than rule 67's: nine unhedged non-conceding units against one, REV.8.9, with the six remaining folds — JHN.11.27, JUD.1.4, 1JN.5.13, JHN.14.17, JHN.14.26 and REV.19.21 — every one of them hedged and three conceding `added`. Where an **anarthrous noun or name** carries it, *even* folds onto that noun as a rule 7 helper headed on the noun: `Χριστοῦ` → *even Christ* at COL.2.2, as `Χριστός` → *even Christ* at EPH.4.15. What empties the article carrier is rule 32's *and nothing else*, which is scoped to an article and reaches no other word, so a bare noun has nothing to keep an ordinary helper out and rule 7 folds it as it folds any other supplied word onto the token that licenses it. Say in the note that marking such an *even* `added` under rule 5 remains defensible: the precedent is two units and EPH.4.15 is hedged, though the corpus carries no `added` bare *even* on a noun carrier anywhere. An **articular** noun is not this case and is the article's, decided above. Rule 24 does not require a chapter writing more than one of these to match them, the carrier classes being different, which is why JAS.4 folds at 4:1 and adds at 4:12. Rule 98 reaches none of these carriers, being scoped in terms to an asyndetic seam between two **like** constituents both rendered alike, and rule 88's juncture principle is not a route to the fold, rule 98 having already scoped it to a circumstantial participle converted into a coordinate finite clause. A supplied *even* answering an expressed `καί` or standing in a correlative is untouched by this rule and is decided by rules 82 and 100, and one the ASV supplies where no appositive follows at all — REV.2.13 `ὅπου` → *even where* — is aligned in the ordinary way.
amendments.why: Rule 105 enumerates two carrier classes and settles each, but a reader whose appositive is carried by a bare noun has nothing to apply. COL.2.2's τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ, Χριστοῦ → the mystery of God, even Christ is that case, and the verse pass had to reason it out from rule 32's scoping. The amendment writes that reasoning into the rule: the article carrier is `added` only because rule 32 restricts an article to its pronoun and nothing else, and that restriction reaches no other word, so a noun takes the helper in the ordinary way. The corpus agrees and does not contradict — EPH.4.15 Χριστός → even Christ is folded and headed on christ, and every `added` bare *even* the rule already lists stands on an article. The evidence is thin, two units and one of them hedged, so the amendment says so and requires the note to name the competing reading rather than presenting the arm as settled.

conventions: A Greek compound noun the ASV renders by two English words that each gloss one of its elements heads on the word answering to the nominal core, not on the one answering to the modifying or prefixed element, and English word order does not move it: πιθανολογίᾳ → persuasiveness of speech heads on speech (COL.2.4, corrected in this pass) as ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ → will worship heads on worship (COL.2.23). Where the second English word is a generic completion rather than a gloss, rule 66's other arm applies and the head goes to the word carrying the sense.

Where the ASV verbalizes εἰς plus a noun, the preposition takes the English word introducing the resulting clause and the noun takes the verb: εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν → that on εἰς and they may know on the noun (COL.2.2), εἰς φθοράν → to on εἰς and perish on the noun (COL.2.22). That is rule 61's placement holding where the preposition governs a nominal rather than an articular infinitive. Leaving the preposition unrepresented and giving the introducer to the noun remains defensible and is named in both verses.

An English preposition standing over an accusative object stays inside the verb's or the frame's unit throughout this chapter — maketh spoil of (2.8), triumphing over (2.15), dwelling in (2.18), increaseth with (2.19) — and where that accusative carries an article of its own the article takes only the bare the the ASV wrote, never with the or of the. Rule 21 gives an article the preposition realizing its noun's own case and an accusative has none, so nothing is left for the article to carry beyond its determiner. COL.2.19 was corrected to this reading and its article now stands on a bare the.

A supplied English correlative or intensifier standing with a comparative that has no answering καί rides with the comparative under rules 7 and 82 and is not added: Ὡς → As … so, discontinuously (COL.2.6), and καθὼς → even as (COL.2.7). Rule 82 gives such a word to the καί only where one stands, and none does in either verse.

report: One real cross-verse split, in compound-noun head placement. COL.2.4 πιθανολογίᾳ → *persuasiveness of speech* headed the modifying element, while COL.2.23 ἐθελοθρησκίᾳ → *will worship* headed the nominal core. Both are one Greek compound noun rendered by two English words each of which glosses one of its elements; nothing in the source licenses the difference, only English word order, which rule 17 forbids as a ground. Rule 91's own rows decide it the other way (καταλαλιάς → *evil speakings* on *speakings*, δυσφημίας → *evil report* on *report*), as do rule 66's εὐδοκία, εὐνοία and εὐαγγέλιον and rule 104's εὐπειθής and εὐάρεστος. COL.2.4's head moved to *speech*, with the competing reading named in the note; nothing else in that verse changed.

Checked and cleared as source-licensed rather than split: the σύν/συν- family (2.2, 2.12 twice, 2.13, 2.19 — *with him* goes to an expressed dative or to an expressed σύν, and rides inside the verb only where the compound governs nothing, which is rule 106's two arms and not two analyses); article plus supplied possessive (displaced and empty at 2.1, 2.5, 2.13, 2.17, 2.18; article takes it at 2.7, 2.8, 2.13, the last on rule 76's availability test); determinerless genitives (of with the noun, article empty, uniformly at 2.2, 2.3, 2.8, 2.11, 2.12, 2.19, 2.22); relative-plus-things heads (2.17, 2.18, 2.22, 2.23, all on *things*); preverb particles (2.7, 2.11, 2.14, 2.18, 2.19, all headed on the verb word); μηδείς heads (2.4, 2.18, both on *no*), 2.16's μή+τις being a different construction with its joined reading already named.

The candidate table is blind to `added` units, so I read the dump end to end for an add-here/fold-there split and found none. The two `added` units — *I say* (2.13) and *but* (2.23) — are supplied lexical content and a supplied conjunction whose licensing token μέν is already spent on *indeed*, which is rule 103's line. Every folded supplied word (*so* at 2.6, *even* at 2.2, *written* at 2.14, resumptive *them* at 2.15, *with him* at 2.12, *your prize* at 2.18) has a token still owing English, so the two sides do not conflict.

BSB: all seven disagreements are article and particle convention differences, not errors. Six are articles the ASV gives no determiner to and rule 23 therefore empties (2.8 τῶν, 2.22 τῶν, 2.12 τῆς, 2.18 τῆς, 2.14 τοῖς) or that a possessive displaces under rule 20 (2.17 τοῦ before Χριστοῦ, the ASV writing *Christ's*); the seventh is the intensifying καί of the concessive εἰ καί at 2.5, which rule 65 leaves empty where the ASV writes no word for it. No accepted edge was changed to move the figure.

Four conventions recorded and two amendments returned, to rules 66 and 105. Rule 66 gains the compound-noun clause this chapter's split turned on; rule 105 gains the anarthrous-noun carrier for the appositional *even*, which its two enumerated carriers left open and which COL.2.2 had to reason out with EPH.4.15 as its only precedent.
